title: Egypt to Indonesia
hookLine: the school is followed in Egypt, East Africa, Yemen and Southeast Asia

lines: A WIND THAT KEEPS A CALENDAR.
CARGO, AND PEOPLE WHO KNEW THE LAW.
cards: A sail fills with a wind that keeps a calendar. For part of the year it blows one way across the Indian Ocean. Then the season turns, and so does the wind.
Sailors timed their lives by it. They loaded cloth and spices and letters, and alongside the cargo they carried people who knew the law. Yesterday's poem said: travel, and you'll find.
The school of al-Shafi'i traveled farther than he ever did. Today, where it went, and what carried it.

teach.b: Start where he ended. Al-Shafi'i spent his last years in Egypt, and his tomb in Cairo still receives visitors. His students there kept his teaching, and from there it spread.
The school is followed in Egypt, along the coast of East Africa, in Yemen, across Southeast Asia in places like Malaysia and Indonesia, and in parts of southern India, like Kerala.
On a map, that's a shape of coastlines: many of these lands ring the Indian Ocean. Much of it went by sea, and by the wind.

teach.h: CARRIED BY TRADERS ON THE MONSOON.
teach.b: The monsoon blows across that water one way for part of the year, then turns back. Merchants from Arabia and Yemen sailed with it to the Swahili coast, to India, to the islands.
They traded, married, settled, built mosques. Some were scholars; families of teachers from Hadramawt, in Yemen, became known for teaching far from home.
When someone in a port town asked how to pray or how to divide an inheritance, the answer came out of the books these travelers carried. The Qur'an points at this kind of traffic.
Among God's signs, it says, are the winds he sends as heralds of his mercy, so that ships may sail at his command and people may seek his bounty, and perhaps be thankful.
A trade wind is an ordinary thing; in that verse, it's a sign. And the books are still read.
In a village school in Java and a mosque on the Kenyan coast, students study manuals of the same school, such as the Minhaj of al-Nawawi. Far apart, the same pages, joined by water.

how: Muslims in Egypt, East Africa, Yemen, parts of southern India and Southeast Asia commonly follow the Shafi'i school, and its manuals are studied in their mosques, schools and seminaries.

games.why: you wait. the monsoon turns with the season, and sailors timed their voyages to it. the school's books rode the same winds.

practice: Picture the Indian Ocean, or open a map, and rest a finger in the middle of the water.

Let your eyes travel slowly around the rim, one breath for each stretch: the Red Sea, the coast of Yemen, East Africa, southern India, the islands to the east, everything facing the same water and waiting on the same wind.
If you pray, you can remember the travelers who carried what they knew.

wordCard.voice: Egypt to Indonesia. The lands of the Shafi'i school, strung around the Indian Ocean, linked by trade and by the monsoon. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: al-Shafi'i, the name of the imam the school is named for.
